Let  $P$  be the foot from  $C$  to  $AB$ , and let  $I$  and  $I_C$  be the centers of  $k$  and  $l$  respectively. Let  $CI \cap AB = Q$ . 
Since  $\angle I_CAI = 90^{\circ}$  and  $\angle QAI = \angle IAC$ , we must have  $(I_C, I; Q, C) = -1$ . 
Note that  $\angle QPC = 90^{\circ}$ , so we must have  $\angle I_CPQ = \angle QPI \iff 90^{\circ} - \angle I_CPQ = 90^{\circ} - \angle QPI \iff \angle I_CPZ = \angle IPY$ .
Note there is a homothety at  $C$  taking  $k$  to  $l$ , which also takes  $I$  to  $I_C$ ,  $X$  to  $Z$ , and  $Y$  to  $T$ , so  $IX \parallel I_CZ$ ,  $IY \parallel I_CT$ , and  $\triangle IXY \sim \triangle I_CZT$ . Together with the fact that  $IX = IY$  and  $I_CZ = I_CT$ , we have  $\angle IYP = 180^{\circ} - \angle IYC = 180^{\circ} - \angle I_CTC = 180^{\circ} - \angle I_CTZ = 180^{\circ} - \angle I_CZT = \angle I_CZP$ .
Thus,  $\triangle IPY \sim \triangle I_CPZ$  and  $\frac{PY}{PZ} = \frac{IY}{I_CZ} = \frac{IY}{I_CT} = \frac{YX}{TZ}$ .
So  $\frac{YX}{PY} = \frac{TZ}{PZ} \iff \frac{PX}{PY} = \frac{PT}{PZ} \iff PX \cdot PZ = PY \cdot PT$ .
Hence,  $PY \cdot PT = PX \cdot PZ = PD \cdot PE$ , so  $D, Y, E, T$  are concyclic.

stem_md:
On the board are written  $n$  natural numbers,  $n\in \mathbb{N}$ . In one move it is possible to choose two 
equal written numbers and increase one by  $1$  and decrease the other by  $1$ . Prove that in this
the game cannot be played more than  $\frac{n^3}{6}$  moves.
solution_md:
Extremely Slick Problem! **Claim 1:** The order of moves does not matter.
ProofSince the number of particular number does not change due to order of moves $\therefore$ the order of moves is irrelevant. $\blacksquare$
Now consider an infinite rectangular grid of dimensions with width 1, Label starting from the first square $1,2 \cdots$ , then write the number of rocks of that number in the cell(square).Notice that the given operation is equivalent to keeping one rock to the right while one to right. Call the leftmost square with atleast $2$ the "pivot" of a given configuration. **Claim 2:** Assume there are $t$ $1$ 's before the "pivot of the config." we can make that $t+1$ in atmost $\frac{(t+1)(t+2)}{2}$ moves.
Proof$0\underbrace{111111}_{t}$ $\rightarrow$ $0\underbrace{11111}_{(t-1)}2(P-2)$ $\rightarrow$ $0\underbrace{1111}_{(t-2)}20(P-1) $ $\rightarrow$ $ 0\underbrace{111}_{(t-3)}201(P-1)$ $\rightarrow $ $0\underbrace{11}_{(t-4)}2011(P-1)$ $\rightarrow$ $10\underbrace{11111}_{(t-1)}(P-1)$ , repeat to get the desired bound
$\sum_{t=0}^{n-2} \frac{(t+1)(t+2)}{2} = \sum_{t=0}^{n-2} \frac{t^2}{2} + \frac{3t}{2}+1 \geq \frac{n^3}{6}$
remark (after 4 months)this is basically 1996 C6 lol

Just a sketch of one possible approach:
First we note that it doesn’t matter in which order the moves are done (proof is pretty simple). Now imagine the numbers are rocks on a infinite grind and the move consists of taking to rocks from the same square and moving one left and one right. We say that the pivot of a configuration is the left most square with at least 2 rocks. And we say that the power of the configuration is the number of rocks to the left of the pivot. I claim, that if the power right now is x, we can increase the power to x+1, by at most (x+1)(x+2)/2 moves. Proof: say there are y adjacent squares  left to the pivot with 1 rock. Notice that by this algorithm we can make that number y-1 by y+1 moves:
01111P -> 01112(P-2) -> 01120(P-1) -> 01201(P-1) -> 02011(P-1) > 10111(P-1)
Hence by (y+1) + (y) + …. +(2) we can make it 0, and then by one more move we increase the power of the configuration. Hence at most (y+2)(y+1)/2 moves were needed.
Now if the power is n-2, we need at most n-1 moves to finish the configuration. Hence the maximum number of moves is (sum(i+2)(i+1)/2)( i=0 to n-3) + (n-1) = n^3/6 - (n^2)/4 + 4/3(n) - 1 which is less than n^3/6 when n is bigger than 4. 

Remark. This is not sharp, for instance one could easily improve the solution by noticing that when the power of configuration is more than n/2, the pivot will probably decrease to 1 before our algorithm finishes.

Actually we can prove the stronger bound $\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{24}$ We proceed by induction on  $n$ .
If  $n=1$ , then everything is clear.
Now assume that the conclusion holds for  $n-1$ . Pick one of these rocks (as in the reformation in the previous solution) and forget about it at first(we can do this since it doesn't matter what order the moves are done). By induction hypothesis, the process terminates in at most  $\frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{24}$  moves. Then put the rock into consideration.and there is at most one grid with more than one rock, (its only possible position is where that rock originally lies)and moreover, if there is such a grid, (WLOG assume that this is the case or the conclusion holds automatically) it must contain 2 rocks. 
Now, consider the first empty grid to the left of it , and assume that there are  $k$  grid(s) between them, and define  $l$  similarly.(for instance, in the configuration 0,1,1,0,2,1,1,1,0,1  $k=0$  and $l=3$ ) then we get that  $$ k+l\le n-2 $$  So it remains to prove the following claim.**Claim.**Let  $k,l$  be nonnegative integers. If the initial configuration is  $0,1,1,...,1,2,1,1,...,1,0$  with  $k$  1s to the left of the 2, and  $l$  1s to the right. then the process terminates after  $(k+1)(l+1)$ steps, and the final configuration is  $1,1,...,1,0,1,1,...,1$ , with  $l+1$  1s to the left of the 0, and  $k+1$  1s to the right.**Proof.** Induct on  $k+l$ .
The claim is obviously true when  $k+l=0$ . Now assume that the claim is true when  $k+l=m-1$ , and consider the case when  $k+l=m$ .
Assume WLOG that k>0.Then we can perform the process as below(an example when  $k=4$  and  $l=2$ ) $0,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,0$  $\rightarrow0,1,1,1,2,0,2,1,0$  $\rightarrow0,1,1,1,2,1,0,2,0$  $\rightarrow0,1,1,1,2,1,1,0,1$ After that it reduces to induction hypothesis and we are done.

The claim together with induction hypothesis implies that the process terminates in at most  $$ \frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{24} +(k+1)(l+1)\le\frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{24}+\frac{n^2}{4} =\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{24} $$  steps and the proof is complete.

stem_md:
The table of dimensions  $n\times n$ ,  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , is filled with numbers from  $1$  to  $n^2$ , but the difference
any two numbers on adjacent fields is at most  $n$ , and that for every  $k = 1, 2,\dots , n^2$  set of fields
whose numbers are  $1, 2,\dots , k$  is connected, as well as the set of fields whose numbers are  $k, k + 1,\dots  , n^2$ . Neighboring fields are fields with a common side, while a set of fields is considered connected if from each field to every other field of that set can be reached going only to the neighboring fields within that set. 
We call a pair of adjacent numbers, ie. numbers on adjacent fields, good, if their absolute difference is exactly  $n$ (one number can be found in several good pairs). Prove that the table has at least  $2 (n - 1)$  good pairs.

stem_md: Let  $p$  and  $q$  be different primes, and  $\alpha\in (0, 3)$  a real number.  Prove that in sequence  $$ \left[ \alpha \right] , \left[ 2\alpha \right] , \left[ 3\alpha \right] \dots $$  exists number less than  $2pq$ , divisible by  $p$  or  $q$ .
solution_md:
Interesting problem, here is a hastily written solution that still took too much time to satisfy impatient AoPSers (I started writing this up after the bump last night even though I solved the problem a couple days ago) :) The fact that  $p,q$  are distinct primes is crucial, of course, one can find arbitrarily long sequences  $\lfloor \alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 2\alpha \rfloor, \cdots$  are not divisible by  $p$  but both non-divisibilities cannot happen for too long.

Replace  $[x]$  by  $\lfloor x \rfloor$  and let  $c \mathbb{N}$  denote the set  $\{cn | n \in \mathbb{N}\}$  (our problem concerns the integer part of  $\alpha \mathbb{N}$  hence this notation). Assume for the sake of contradiction that there are  $\alpha \in (0,3)$  and  $p,q$  distinct primes that do not satisfy the condition. 

Firstly, assume that  $\alpha > 1$  because otherwise, as a multiset,  $\mathbb{N} \subset \{\lfloor \alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 2 \alpha \rfloor, \cdots\}$ .

Now, the main idea, consider  $m_p = \lfloor \frac{p}{\alpha} \rfloor $  and  $m_q = \lfloor \frac{q}{\alpha} \rfloor$  and  $s_p = p-\alpha \cdot m_p$  and  $m_q = q - \alpha \cdot m_q$ <details><summary>Overall Idea Applied After Lemma 1</summary>We will see how  $s_p$  and  $s_q$  add up over time and will show that eventually one of the two quantities  $k_1p-\lfloor \frac{k_1p}{\alpha} \rfloor$  or  $k_2q-\lfloor \frac{k_2q}{\alpha} \rfloor$  for  $k_1 \in \{1, \cdots, 2q\}$  or  $k_2 \in \{1, \cdots, 2p\}$  will get too large (specifically, one such number will exceed  $\alpha-1$ ), which will finish because then adding  $\alpha$  to said number will remain in  $\alpha \mathbb{N}$  and have integer part divisible by one of our two primes.</details> $\textbf{Lemma 1:}$  Either  $s_p > \frac{1}{q}$  or  $s_q > \frac{1}{p}$ <details><summary>Motivation: Working Backwards</summary>This lemma may seem out of the blue and there is in fact a different lemma that one is motivated to prove, this is by working backwards, that is if the problem holds, then the following **Lemma 1'** must hold.**Lemma 1':**
Either  $s_p > \frac{1}{2q}$  or  $s_q > \frac{1}{2p}$ This must indeed hold for  $\alpha > 2$  because otherwise if we have  $s_p \leq \frac{1}{2q}, s_q < \frac{1}{2p}$ , then  $k_1p-\alpha \cdot \lfloor \frac{k_1p}{\alpha} \rfloor < 1$  for all  $k_1 \in \{1, \cdots, 2q\}$  and similarly  $k_2q-\alpha \cdot \lfloor \frac{k_2q}{\alpha} \rfloor < 1$  for all  $k_2 \in \{1, \cdots, 2p\}$  and hence there is in this case no  $i \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $\lfloor i \cdot \alpha \rfloor < 2pq$  and divisible by either  $p$  or  $q$ . 

Now, once one tries proving **Lemma 1'**, one realizes that in fact the stronger **Lemma 1** holds as well.</details>

Now, we shall prove the lemma.**Proof)** 
Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $s_p \leq \frac{1}{q}, s_q \leq \frac{1}{p}$ . Our idea is to double count  $\lfloor \frac{pq}{\alpha} \rfloor$  and notice that  $S_q = q \cdot \lfloor \frac{p}{\alpha} \rfloor \cdot \alpha = q(p-s_p) = qp-qs_p \in (pq-1,pq)$ , this is because clearly  $pq > qp-qs_p \geq qp-1$  because  $qs_p \leq 1$  by our assumption and furthermore  $(q \cdot \lfloor \frac{p}{\alpha} \rfloor) \cdot \alpha \in \alpha\mathbb{N}$  which means that  $S_q = \lfloor \frac{pq}{\alpha} \rfloor$ , analogously,   $$ pq-qs_p = S_p = \lfloor \frac{pq}{\alpha} \rfloor= S_q = pq-ps_q $$   this allows us to conclude that   $$ qs_p = ps_q \qquad (\clubsuit) $$   Now, we can go back to our definitions,   $$ \frac{p-s_p}{m_p} = \alpha = \frac{q-s_q}{m_p} = \frac{q-\frac{qs_p}{p}}{m_q} $$   by  $(\clubsuit)$  which upon rearrangement gives us that  $qm_p = pm_q$ , then as  $q > \frac{q}{\alpha} \geq m_q$ , we know that  $gcd(q,m_q) = gcd(q,p) = 1$  because  $p,q$  are distinct primes which contradicts the fact that  $q \mid pm_q$ .  $\blacksquare$  

We will now finish in the case when without loss of generality  $s_p >1, \alpha > 2$  (the second inequality must hold, that is, if  $s_p >1, \alpha < 2$  we can indeed finish, these cases will be added to the end of the proof as they are not the main ingredients of the solution and don't need emphasis), the case  $s_q, s_p \leq 1$  will be easy to deal with later as well. Notice firstly, that  $\alpha-1 > s_p>\alpha-1-s_p$  and that  $kp- \lfloor \frac{kp}{\alpha} \rfloor \cdot \alpha$  alternates in between the intervals  $(\alpha-s_p,\alpha-1)$  and  $(0,\alpha-s_p-1)$  increasing by  $M_p = 2s_p-\alpha$ , now, we repeat  $\textbf{Lemma 1}$  but in this case we double count  $2pq - \lfloor \frac{2pq}{\alpha} \rfloor \cdot \alpha$  instead.

We will split into cases.  $\textbf{Case 1:}$   $s_q < \frac{1}{p}$  
In this case we have that  $M_pq = 2pq-\lfloor \frac{2pq}{\alpha} \rfloor =  2s_qp$  and   $$ \frac{2p-M_p}{T_1} = \alpha = \frac{2q-2s_q}{T_2} = \frac{2q-\frac{M_pq}{p}}{T_2} $$   for  $T_1, T_2 \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $T_1 < \frac{2p}{\alpha} < p, T_2  < \frac{2q}{\alpha} < q$  because  $\alpha > 2$  which gives us that  $pT_2 = qT_1$  contradicting the fact that  $p,q$  are distinct primes. $\textbf{Case 2:}$   $s_q  > 1$  
Now, we have the same conclusions as for  $s_p > 1$ , that is if  $M_q = 2\alpha-s_q$ , then  $M_q = 2q- \lfloor \frac{2q}{\alpha} \rfloor \cdot \alpha$ , then we can again double count  $\lfloor \frac{2pq}{\alpha} \rfloor$  as  $M_pq = M_qp$  because we know that  $f(k) = kq- \lfloor \frac{kq}{\alpha} \rfloor \cdot \alpha$  alternates in between the intervals  $f(i) \in (\alpha-s_q,\alpha-1)$  for odd  $i$  and  $f(j) \in (0,\alpha-s_q-1)$  even  $j$  increasing by  $M_q$  at each even step that is  $f(k+2) = f(k)+M_q$ , otherwise, we can find some  $i \in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $q \mid \lfloor i \cdot \alpha \rfloor < 2pq$ . 

This implies again that there are  $T_1, T_2 \in \mathbb{N}$  with  $T_1 < \frac{2p}{\alpha} < p, T_2 < \frac{2q}{\alpha} < q$  such that   $$ \frac{2p-M_p}{T_1} = \alpha = \frac{2q-M_q}{T_2} = \frac{2q-\frac{M_pq}{p}}{T_2} $$   which implies that  $pT_2 = qT_1$ , again contradicting the fact that  $p,q$  are distinct primes as  $T_1 < p, T_2 < q$ .  $\blacksquare$  

<details><summary>Less Emphasis Worthy Cases</summary>We have the two cases  $s_p > 1, \alpha < 2$  and  $s_p, s_q \leq 1$  to deal with. **Case 1)**  $s_p > 1, \alpha \leq 2$ Then  $\alpha-1< s_p$  because otherwise  $1 > \alpha-1 \geq s_p > 1$  which is a contradiction.**Case 2)**  $s_p, s_q < 1$ This case is the reason we proved  $\textbf{Lemma 1}$ , notice that, we know by the aforementioned lemma that either  $s_p > \frac{1}{q}$  or  $s_q > \frac{1}{p}$ , without loss of generality the former holds, then  $2qs_p > 2 \geq \alpha-1$ , then, say by Discrete Continuitity there must be be some  $i \in \{1, \cdots, 2q\}$  such that  $i \cdot s_p \in (\alpha-1, \alpha)$  because  $s_p < 1$  and  $2qs_p > \alpha-1$ .</details>

The case where  $p=2$  implies the sequence will contain all odd numbers up to  $4q$ , so assume  $p,q\ge 3$ .

For laziness, replace  $\alpha$  with  $a$ . Note  $p|[ta] \leftrightarrow \left\{ \frac{ta}{p} \right\} < \frac 1p$ Let  $t_p$  be the minimal number such that  $\{ \frac{(t+1)a}{p} \} > \{ \frac{ta}{p}\}$ , and let   $$ S_p=\left\{ t| \left\{ \frac{(t+1)a}{p} \right\} > \left\{ \frac{ta}{p} \right\} \text{ and } (t+1)a < 2pq\right\} $$  The key is to bound  $\frac tp a$  or  $\frac{t+1}{p}a$  closely, and then use a similar bound for  $q$  to derive a contradiction. 

Case 1: Not all elements in  $S_p$  are divisible by  $t_p$ .

Claim:  $2t\notin S_p$ .

Proof: Let  $m$  be the minimal integer such that  $mt\notin S, (m-1)t\in S\rightarrow mt+1\in S$ .

Let  $\epsilon=1-\left\{ \frac{ta}{p} \right\}$ . From $(m-1)t\in S \rightarrow 1-(m-1)\epsilon = \{ \frac{(m-1)ta}{p} \} > 1-\frac{a-1}{p}$ . This implies  $\epsilon < \frac{a-1}{p(m-1)}$  $mt\notin S \rightarrow \epsilon > \frac{a}{pm}$ .

This implies  $\frac{m}{m-1} > \frac{a}{a-1}$ , so  $a>m$ , which means  $m=2$  is forced, proving our claim. 

Let  $J=\frac{(t+1)a}{p}-1$ . Then, note  $\frac 1p < J < \frac{a}{2p}$  because  $2t+1\in S \rightarrow 2J<\frac ap$ . Therefore,  $0<\frac{3-a}{p} < 3J-\frac ap < \frac{a}{2p}$ , which implies  $\frac 1p < 3J-\frac ap < \frac{a}{2p}$  if  $(3(t+1)-1)a < 2pq$ . Repeating the same argument yields  $\frac 1p < (2n+1)J-n\frac ap < \frac{a}{2p}$  if  $((2n+1)(t+1)-n)a<2pq$ We get  $\frac{2t+1}{2p} a - 1 \in \left( \frac{2-a}{(4n+2)p}, 0 \right)$  if  $n(2t+1)+(t+1) < \frac{2pq}{a}$ . Since  $n(2t+1)<2p$ , we can get  $n\ge q-1$ Case 2: all elements in  $S_p$  are a multiple of  $t_p$ .

Let  $\epsilon = 1-\{ \frac{ta}{p} \}$  Note  $\{ \frac{mta}{p} \} =1-m\epsilon$ . Pick the largest  $m$  such that  $(mt+1)a< 2pq$ . Since  $ta<p$  it follows that  $m\ge 2q-1$ . We also have  $\{ \frac{(mt+1)a}{p} \} > \frac 1p$ , which means  $1-(2q-1)\epsilon < 1 - \frac{a-1}{p}$  so  $\epsilon<\frac{a-1}{p(2q-1)}$ This means   $$ 1>\frac tp \cdot a > 1 - \frac{a-1}{p(2q-1)} $$  Now we combine the same bound for  $q$ . $a$  falls into case 1 for  $p,q$ : for some  $t,u$ ,  $(\frac{2t+1}{2p} - \frac{2u+1}{2q})a < \frac{a-2}{(4q-2)p}$  but LHS  $\ge \frac{a}{2pq}$ , impossible. $a$  falls into case 1 for  $p$ , case 2 for  $q$ : analogously we get  $\frac{a}{2pq}<\frac{a-2}{(4q-2)p} +\frac{a-1}{p(2q-1)}$ , impossible if  $a<3$  $a$  falls into case 2 for  $p,q$ :  $\frac{a}{pq} < \frac{a-1}{p(2q-1)}$ .

All three cases are impossible. The conclusion follows.

Assume for the sake of contradiction there does not exist any number in  $\left[ \alpha \right] , \left[ 2\alpha \right] , \left[ 3\alpha \right] \dots$  less than  $2pq$  and divisible by  $p$  or  $q$ . WLOG assume  $p < q$ . Then  $q$  must be odd.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, among the integers  $1,2,\ldots,pq$  there exist two consecutive numbers  $a, a+1$  that are divisible by  $p$  and  $q$  respectively. We may assume  $a\le \dfrac{pq}{2}$ ; otherwise consider  $pq-a-1, pq-a$ . If  $p \ne 2$  and  $a = \dfrac{pq-1}{2}$ , then  $2p \mid pq -1 \Rightarrow p \mid 1$ , contradiction. If  $p = 2$  and  $a = \dfrac{pq}{2} = q$ , then  $2 \mid q$ , contradiction. Hence, we must have  $a < \dfrac{pq - 1}{2}$ .

Let  $A=\{\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor\mid n\in\mathbb{N}\}\cap(0,2pq)$ . By assumption,  $a,a+1\notin A$ . Since  $\alpha<3$ , we have  $\lfloor (n+1)\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor \le \lfloor\alpha\rfloor+1\le 3$ , hence among any three consecutive positive integers there must be at least one that belongs to  $A$ . Therefore  $a-1, a+2\in A$ .

Since  $q \mid pq-a-1$  and  $p \mid pq - a$ , we must have  $pq-a-2\in A$ . Since  $q \mid pq+a+1$  and  $p \mid pq + a$ , we must have  $pq+a-1\in A$ .  Since  $q \mid 2pq-a-1$  and  $p \mid 2pq - a$ , we must have  $2pq-a-2\in A$ . It is easy to check that \[a - 1 < pq - a - 2 < pq + a - 1 < 2pq - a - 2,\] so there exist positive integers  $n_1<n_2<n_3<n_4$  such that \[\lfloor n_1\alpha\rfloor=a-1, \lfloor n_2\alpha\rfloor=pq-a-2, \lfloor n_3\alpha\rfloor=pq+a-1, \lfloor n_4\alpha\rfloor=2pq-a-2.\]

We proceed to use the following lemma:**Lemma:** For any reals  $x, y$ ,  $\lfloor x - y \rfloor$  is  $\lfloor x \rfloor - \lfloor y \rfloor - 1$  iff  $\{x\} < \{y\}$ , and  $\lfloor x \rfloor - \lfloor y \rfloor$  otherwise. 
<details><summary>Proof of Lemma</summary>Note that  $\lfloor x - y \rfloor = \lfloor \lfloor x \rfloor + \{x\} - \lfloor y \rfloor - \{y\} \rfloor  = \lfloor x \rfloor - \lfloor y \rfloor + \lfloor \{x\} - \{y\} \rfloor$ . Since  $0 \le \{x\}, \{y\} < 1$ , we must have  $-1 < \{x\} - \{y\} < 1$ . So if  $\{x\} < \{y\}$ , then  $\lfloor \{x\} - \{y\} \rfloor = -1$ , otherwise,  $\lfloor \{x\} - \{y\} \rfloor = 0$ . This completes the proof of the lemma.</details>

Because  $\lfloor n_3\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_1\alpha\rfloor=pq$ , and by assumption  $\lfloor (n_3-n_1)\alpha\rfloor$  is not divisible by  $p$  or  $q$ , we obtain  $\big\lfloor (n_3-n_1)\alpha\big\rfloor = \lfloor n_3\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_1\alpha\rfloor - 1$ , hence  $\{n_3\alpha\}<\{n_1\alpha\}$ . Likewise,  $\{n_4\alpha\}<\{n_2\alpha\}$ .

Next, since  $\lfloor n_3\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_2\alpha\rfloor = 2a+1$ , and by assumption  $\lfloor (n_3-n_2)\alpha\rfloor$  is not divisible by  $p$  or  $q$ , while  $2a$  is divisible by  $p$ , it follows that  $\big\lfloor (n_3-n_2)\alpha\big\rfloor = \lfloor n_3\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_2\alpha\rfloor$ , implying  $\{n_3\alpha\}\ge \{n_2\alpha\}$ .

Similarly,  $\lfloor n_4\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_1\alpha\rfloor = 2pq-2a-1$ , and by assumption  $\lfloor (n_4-n_1)\alpha\rfloor$  is not divisible by  $p$  or  $q$ , whereas  $2pq-2a-2$  is divisible by  $q$ . Hence  $\big\lfloor (n_4-n_1)\alpha\big\rfloor = \lfloor n_4\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor n_1\alpha\rfloor$ , and thus  $\{n_4\alpha\}\ge \{n_1\alpha\}$ .

Combining the four inequalities yields  $\{n_1\alpha\}>\{n_3\alpha\}\ge \{n_2\alpha\}>\{n_4\alpha\}\ge\{n_1\alpha\}$ , which is a contradiction and we are done.  $\Box$

stem_md: Let  $n>3$  be a positive integer. Prove that  $n$  is prime if and only if there exists a positive integer  $\alpha$  such that  $n!=n(n-1)(\alpha n+1)$ .
solution_md:
First, suppose  $n$  is a prime. Then,  $(n-1)!\equiv -1\pmod{n}$ , yielding  $(n-2)!\equiv 1\pmod{n}$  by Wilson's theorem. So,  $(n-2)!=\alpha n+1$  for some  $\alpha$ , i.e.,  $n!=n(n-1)(\alpha n+1)$ . 

Conversely, suppose  $(n-2)! = \alpha n +1$  and that  $n$  is not a prime. Write  $n=n_1n_2$  where  $n_1,n_2\ge 2$ . Check that  $n-2 = n_1n_2-2\ge 2n_1-2\ge n_1$  and likewise  $n_1n_2-2\ge 2n_2-2$ . So,  $n_1\mid (n-2)!$  and  $n_2\mid (n-2)!$ . We are done if  $n_1\ne n_2$ . On the other hand, if  $n_1=n_2$  then  $n=n_1^2$  so  $n-2 = n_1^2 -2$  is divisible by both  $n_1$  and  $2n_1$  for  $n_1\ge 3$ . The case  $n=4$  is handled manually, completing the proof.

stem_md: Find the minimum and maximum values of the function  $$ f(x,y,z,t)=\frac{ax^2+by^2}{ax+by}+\frac{az^2+bt^2}{az+bt},~(a>0,b>0), $$  given that  $x+z=y+t=1$ , and  $x,y,z,t\ge0$ .
solution_md:
I will prove that  $1\le f(x,y,z,t)\le 2$  for all such  $x,y,z,t$ ; where for the equality cases take (a)  $x=y=z=t=1/2$  for the left hand side, and (b)  $x=t=1$  and  $y=z=0$  for the right hand side.

We start by  $\ge 1$  case. By Cauchy-Schwarz,
\[
\left(ax^2+by^2\right)(a+b)\ge (ax+by)^2 \implies \frac{ax^2+by^2}{a+b}\ge \frac{ax+by}{a+b}.
\]
Consequently, we obtain that
\[
f(x,y,z,t)\ge \frac{a}{a+b}(x+z)+\frac{b}{a+b}(y+t)=1.
\]
We now prove  $\le 2$  case. Notice that
\[
\frac{ax^2+by^2}{ax+by}\le \max\{x,y\}.
\]
Hence,
\[
f(x,y,z,t)\le \max\{x,y\}+\max\{z,t\}=\max\{x,y\}+\max\{1-x,1-y\}.
\]
Assuming  $x\ge y$ , we find  $f(x,y,z,t)\le x+1-y \le 2$  as  $x-y\le 1$ . The case,  $y\ge x$ , gives analogous conclusion. This establishes  $1\le f(x,y,z,t)\le 2$  for every such quadruple. As we already established the equality cases are attainable, we complete the proof.

stem_md: Determine the set of all real numbers  $\alpha$  with the following property: For each positive  $c$  there exists a rational number  $\frac mn~(m\in\mathbb Z,n\in\mathbb N)$  different than  $\alpha$  such that  $$ \left|\alpha-\frac mn\right|<\frac cn. $$
solution_md:
<details><summary>equivalent form of the given property</summary>Multiplying by  $n$  and reducing modulo  $1$ , the given property is equivalent to
\[
\forall c>0, \exists n\in\mathbb{N}\,:\,\{\alpha n\}\in(0,c)\cup(1-c,1).
\]
Note that  $\{\alpha n\}=0$  is excluded because it's equivalent to  $\alpha=\tfrac{m}n$ , which we're told is disallowed.</details>

<details><summary>irrationals work</summary>If  $\alpha\notin\mathbb{Q}$  then the sequence  $\{\alpha\},\{2\alpha\},\{3\alpha\},\ldots$  is dense in  $(0,1)$ , so the property is true.</details>

<details><summary>rationals fail</summary>If  $\alpha=\tfrac{a}b\in\mathbb{Q}$  then the sequence  $\{\alpha\},\{2\alpha\},\{3\alpha\},\ldots$  never enters  $(0,\tfrac{1}b)\cup(1-\tfrac{1}b,1)$ , so the property is falsified by  $c=\tfrac{1}b$ .

Finally, if  $\alpha=0$  then the sequence  $\{\alpha\},\{2\alpha\},\{3\alpha\},\ldots$  is all zeroes, so the property is falsified by any  $c>0$ .</details>

stem_md: Determine all  $6$ -tuples  $(p,q,r,x,y,z)$  where  $p,q,r$  are prime, and  $x,y,z$  natural numbers such that  $p^{2x}=q^yr^z+1$ .
solution_md:
Write as  $(p^x-1)(p^x+1)=q^yr^z$ .**i)**  $p=2$ . Both  $q$  and  $r$  will be odd and  $\text{gcd} (2^x-1, 2^x+1)=1$ .  $2^x+1>2^x-1$ , so we have three cases:  $2^x-1=1$  which clearly results with the solutions  $(2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 0), (2, 3, 3, 1, 0, 1)$ ,  $2^x-1=q^y$  and  $2^x-1=r^z$  (This last case is the same as the second one so I will not examine it again.)
We have  $2^x-1=q^y$  and  $2^x+1=r^z$  for now.  $x=1$  can be examined as we did above. Let  $x>1$ . Assume  $y>1$ . Then by Catalan's we do not have solution for  $2^x-q^y=1 \Rightarrow y=1$ . Now assume that  $z>1$ . We have  $r^z-2^x=1$  and by Catalan's again we have  $r=3, z=2, x=3$  and we get to the solution  $(2, 7, 3, 3, 1, 2)$ . At last we are left with  $z=1$ . However if both  $2^x-1$  and  $2^x+1$  are primes then by examining at  $\text{mod 3}$  we reach  $x=2$  which gives us the solution  $(2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 1)$ . 
Overall, all solutions from  $p=2$  are from the set  $\{ (2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 0), (2, 3, 3, 1, 0, 1), (2, 7, 3, 3, 1, 2), (2, 3, 7, 3, 2, 1), (2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 1), (2, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1) \}$ **ii)**  $p>2$ . Then  $p^x-1$  will be even but there is no  $2$  factor at  $q^yr^z$  which is a clear contradiction. 

Thus all the cases are examined.
